item.title: SharePoint CVE-2026-50522 Exploited as Oracle CPU, Azure Extension Abuse, Anubis Fairlife Attack Emerge
item.content:encoded:
Critical SharePoint RCE flaw exploited to steal machine keys — Must Read

Attackers are actively exploiting the critical Microsoft SharePoint RCE flaw CVE-2026-50522 to steal machine keys, enabling them to forge authentication tokens and maintain access even after servers are patched. Organizations should apply the July security updates and rotate exposed credentials or keys.

  • Hackers are actively exploiting the critical CVE-2026-50522 vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint to steal machine keys and maintain access even after affected servers are patched.
  • Microsoft describes CVE-2026-50522 as a deserialization-of-untrusted-data flaw that allows a remote attacker to execute code over a network without authentication.
  • Microsoft addressed the flaw in its July security updates, but the advisory did not mark it as actively exploited and noted an increased likelihood of exploitation.
  • watchTowr observed exploitation attempts against on-premise vulnerable SharePoint deployments shortly after proof-of-concept exploit code became public.
  • At least one PowerShell demonstrative exploit for CVE-2026-50522 is available on GitHub and attempts to trigger remote code execution through SharePoint's '/_trust/default.aspx' endpoint.

Oracle July 2026 Critical Patch Update Addresses 1235 CVEs — Must Read

Oracle’s July 2026 Critical Patch Update fixes 1,235 CVEs across 32 product families with 1,449 security patches, including 261 critical updates. Oracle E-Business Suite and Fusion Middleware received the most fixes, so affected customers should prioritize applying the relevant patches.

  • Oracle’s July 2026 Critical Patch Update contains fixes for 1,235 unique CVEs in 1,449 security updates across 32 Oracle product families.
  • The update includes 261 critical patches across 228 CVEs, representing 18% of all patches in the release.
  • High severity patches accounted for 52.7% of the security patches, followed by medium severity patches at 24.7%.
  • Oracle E-Business Suite received the highest number of patches with 410, accounting for 28.3% of all patches.
  • Oracle Fusion Middleware received 355 patches, accounting for 24.5% of all patches.

Anubis ransomware claims Coca-Cola Fairlife attack, threatens data leak — Must Read

The Anubis ransomware gang claims it attacked Coca-Cola’s Fairlife subsidiary, encrypted its Nutanix systems, and stole about 1 TB of corporate data. The group is threatening to leak the data unless Fairlife negotiates, while Coca-Cola has declined to comment on the claims.

  • The Anubis ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the cyberattack on Coca-Cola’s Fairlife dairy subsidiary and threatened to publish allegedly stolen corporate data unless the company pays a ransom.
  • Coca-Cola disclosed on July 16 that a ransomware attack disrupted Fairlife’s operations and forced the company to suspend production at its U.S. facilities.
  • Coca-Cola said attackers gained unauthorized access to part of Fairlife’s systems, including production-related systems, but product quality and safety were not affected and Canadian production continued normally.
  • Anubis claimed it encrypted Fairlife’s Nutanix infrastructure and stole approximately one terabyte of corporate data during the attack.
  • BleepingComputer could not independently verify Anubis’s claims about data theft, system encryption, or the amount of data allegedly stolen, and Coca-Cola declined to comment on the claims.

The Procurement Trap: Inside an AiTM Campaign Targeting Global Institutions — Should Read

Infoblox uncovered a sophisticated adversary-in-the-middle phishing campaign using compromised aged domains, fake procurement/document portals, CAPTCHAs, and cloned Microsoft login pages to steal MFA-protected session tokens from universities, enterprises, and global institutions. The key takeaway is that MFA alone is not enough when attackers can proxy legitimate authentication flows and hijack authenticated sessions.

  • Infoblox analyzed an adversary-in-the-middle phishing campaign that targets universities, enterprises, multinational institutions, and European Union and United Nations agencies with project-themed lures.
  • The campaign uses emails sent from compromised organizational accounts and themes such as requests for information, bid invitations, and shared project documentation to increase credibility.
  • Victims are led through fake document download pages, email prompts, CAPTCHA or Cloudflare Turnstile checks, and cloned authentication pages impersonating services such as Microsoft, OpenGov, ConstructConnect, and European financial institutions.
  • The actor uses multiple adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits, including EvilProxy, FlowerStorm/Storm-1167, and Kali365, to capture credentials, session cookies, authentication tokens, and MFA-protected access in real time.
  • The campaign relies on aged and likely compromised domains, including examples such as testserveren.com and barifurniture.net, to host fake document download pages and evade reputation-based detection.

Apple Fixes Hide My Email Bug That Exposed Real Addresses in Mail Logs — Should Read

Apple fixed a Hide My Email flaw that could expose users’ real email addresses in mail server logs when messages to their masked addresses were rejected as spam. The bug had been reported over a year earlier and may have leaked addresses tied to Hide My Email aliases created before July 2026.

  • Apple deployed a fix on July 3, 2026 for a flaw in its Hide My Email service that could expose users’ real email addresses.
  • The issue was reported to Apple on June 13, 2025 by Tyler Murphy, co-founder of EasyOptOuts, and Apple’s earlier patch attempts in March 2026 and June 30, 2026 were unsuccessful.
  • The flaw could cause a user’s real email address to appear in email logs when a message sent to their Hide My Email address was rejected as spam.
  • Real email addresses linked to Hide My Email addresses created before July 7, 2026 may have been captured in mail transfer logs when non-malicious emails bounced.
  • Apple is facing a class action lawsuit alleging it misled customers about the privacy of Hide My Email while charging for the feature.

DNI nominee Clayton wins Senate panel’s approval — May Read

The Senate Intelligence Committee approved Jay Clayton’s nomination for director of national intelligence in a party-line vote, sending it to the full Senate. His confirmation could affect stalled efforts to renew Section 702 surveillance authority, which lapsed amid Democratic objections to the acting intelligence chief.

  • The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 9-8 along party lines to support President Donald Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton.
  • The vote clears the way for the full Senate to decide whether to confirm Clayton, likely before senators leave for the August recess.
  • Committee Democrats raised concerns during Clayton’s confirmation hearing that he would politicize the position on Trump’s behalf after he refused to acknowledge that Joe Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election, saying only that Biden was “certified.”
  • Clayton testified that he had no involvement with Trump’s national primetime address accusing some foreign countries, particularly China, of trying to interfere in American elections.
  • Clayton’s confirmation could potentially clear the way for bipartisan legislation to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which expired last month.

Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Chef — Optional

The article shows how an attacker with Azure VM extension write permissions can abuse the legitimate Chef extension to connect a VM to a rogue Chef server and execute arbitrary code, including stealing managed identity tokens. Defenders should tightly restrict VM extension permissions and monitor Azure Activity Logs and Chef-related host logs for unexpected Chef installations or unknown Chef server URLs.

  • An attacker with Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write permission can deploy legitimate third-party Azure VM extensions and configure them to achieve arbitrary code execution on virtual machines.
  • The article demonstrates a rogue Chef server attack in which a target Azure VM installs the Chef extension, registers with an attacker-controlled Chef server, pulls a malicious cookbook, and executes the payload as root.
  • The demonstration cookbook captures an access token for the Managed Identity attached to the VM and sends it to an out-of-band interaction tool.
  • Built-in Azure roles with the permissions needed for this attack include Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, Virtual Machine Contributor, and several less commonly used roles such as VM Restore Operator and Defender Servers P1 and P2.
  • Detection opportunities include monitoring Azure Activity Log events for Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write and reviewing Chef-related log files to identify the Chef server URL and cookbook activity.

Tyro's CISO: Being the "Einstein of cybersecurity" isn't enough if developers don't trust you — Optional

Tyro CISO Arun Singh argues that security teams must protect developer workflows without burning trust, because even technically sound controls can fail if developers see them as productivity blockers. He highlights supply chain defenses like delaying new package updates and using in-IDE/device protection tools that reduce friction.

  • Arun Singh says that being highly skilled in cybersecurity is not enough if a security leader cannot influence the business and earn developer trust.
  • Singh’s earlier removal of local administrator rights across all workstations disrupted software engineers’ productivity and took about a year of trust-building to recover from.
  • Tyro’s recent board conversations have focused on supply chain attacks, where attackers can exploit the long-standing advice for developers to keep packages and dependencies up to date.
  • Singh’s team now advocates a 7-day cooldown period before adopting any new package version, and they held workshops with engineering teams to explain the reasoning.
  • Singh says security tools should fit developer workflows, including in-IDE vulnerability detection and device protection that can block malicious packages, browser extensions, and IDE plugins at install time.
